newsitem.title: MEXICO: Zedillo slams violence, promises advances in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Zedillo slams violence, promises advances in 1997.

text.p: Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo denounced political violence in his annual New Year's address to the nation on Monday, saying that 1997 will be a year of firm democratic and economic advances in Mexico.
"Our democracy is proving that voting and not violence is the way Mexicans have chosen to define the course of the country," Zedillo said.
Zedillo, 45, an economist who has been predsident for 25 months, was referring to the emergence of several self-proclaimed guerrilla armies in 1996.
Only one of the new groups has carried out any military attacks, but all have decried the growing gap between rich and poor as well as corruption in the Mexican political system.
"I have good reason to believe that 1997 will be a year of firm advances for Mexico and for all Mexicans," Zedillo said in a message broadcast nationally on television and radio.
"I have the unbreakable commitment to continue pushing this democratic advance," he added.

Zedillo's claim will be put to the test in July, when midterm congressional elections are held. That's when, according to some polls and political analysts, his ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) is in danger of losing its majority in Congress.
The PRI has held the presidency and dominated Congress for 67 years, but opposition parties have made big gains in local and state gubernatorial elections in recent years.

Earlier Monday, during a visit to the city of Jalapa in the Gulf Coast state of Veracruz, Zedillo rejected the assertion by opponnents that Mexico is in a permanent state of crisis and needs a strong-armed leader to govern.

"Mexico does have its problems, but it is not as some wish to see it, a country irretrievably bogged down in crisis," Zedillo said. "We know it is fortunately only a minority that always sees everything in a pessimistic light."
